analysis.one_liner: Creates a national health insurance program covering doctor, dental, and hospital care, funded by a new 5% national sales tax.
analysis.headline: Dingell's national health insurance bill drew no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote, and died when the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set up a national health insurance program paying for doctor visits, dental care, hospital stays, home nursing, eyeglasses, and expensive drugs. People who qualified through a work history (and their dependents) could choose any participating doctor with no insurance network in between, and Medicare patients could use it to fill gaps in their Medicare coverage. It would have been funded by a new 5% value-added tax on most sales and services, with the money going into a dedicated federal trust fund.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families who meet the bill's wage-history rules would get prepaid coverage for medical, dental, podiatric, home-nursing, hospital, and certain auxiliary services (including unusually expensive drugs and eyeglasses) with free choice of any participating provider. Medicare enrollees could use the program to fill Medicare's gaps, including deductibles and coinsurance. Poor individuals not otherwise eligible could be covered when state or local public agencies reimburse the fund. Providers who join get guaranteed payment and a universal patient pool.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers meeting wage rules, and their families

how_it_helps.text: Provides prepaid personal health services — medical, dental, podiatric, home-nursing, hospital, and auxiliary services such as lab work, expensive drugs, and eyeglasses — to eligible individuals in every health-service area.
Lets every eligible person freely choose any physician, dentist, or hospital that has agreed to furnish services, with free choice of doctor as an explicit policy of the act.
Guarantees services without discrimination based on race, creed, or color, and requires local committees representing patients to run administration.

Allows Medicare beneficiaries to use the program for services Medicare does not cover or where Medicare deductibles and coinsurance apply, and orders a study of eventually folding Medicare into the new program.
Extends the same-quality services to noninsured needy individuals when public agencies reimburse the fund, using federal Medicaid and welfare grant dollars for that purpose.

analysis.who_pays: A new 5% value-added tax on nearly all sales of property and services in the United States, which would raise prices consumers pay, though food, housing, medical care, interest, exports, and governments are exempted. Doctors, dentists, and hospitals that join would accept board- and state-set payment rates, and hospitals would generally be paid at the least expensive multiple-bed rate. Businesses would collect and remit the tax on commercial transactions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers through a new 5% sales tax

drawbacks.text: The 5% value-added tax would be a broad consumption tax on most goods and services; even with food, housing, and medical care exempted, it falls on everyday purchases and does not scale with wealth.
Coverage would not be universal: eligibility hinges on a recent work history or a benefit/annuity entitlement, so people outside the workforce are covered only if a public agency pays for them.

Where personnel, facilities, or funds are inadequate, the Board could limit or scale back dental, home-nursing, and auxiliary services for a period, and hospital stays are capped at 60 days per year with no coverage of mental-disease hospitalization beyond 30 days after a psychosis diagnosis.
Payment rates for professionals and hospitals would be set by the Board, states, and fee schedules rather than the market, which providers argued would hold down incomes and hospital revenue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a real coverage guarantee with free choice of doctor — a stronger consumer position than private insurance networks — and it taxed consumption broadly rather than exempting the wealthy from funding it. But its design had real limits: a work-history eligibility test leaves out people outside the labor force, coverage of some services is explicitly made contingent on available funds and personnel, and a new national consumption tax is a heavy lift for household budgets even with essentials exempted. It was a social-insurance framework from an earlier era (it echoes 1940s Wagner-Murray-Dingell proposals) rather than a fully modern single-payer design.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees on the day it was introduced, then to the Health Subcommittee three weeks later, and neither committee ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative John Dingell introduced the National Health Insurance Act on January 4, 2005, the first day of the 109th Congress.
It attracted zero cosponsors for the entire two-year Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees the day it was introduced, and on January 25, 2005, referred to the Subcommittee on Health.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing health-insurance arrangement was untouched: private insurers kept their role and premiums, employers and consumers never faced the new tax, and no member other than the sponsor ever had to take a position on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The existing private insurance system, unchanged

for.name: Rep. John D. Dingell
for.role: U.S. Representative, Michigan's 15th district; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Health Insurance Act on the first day of the 109th Congress and carried it alone, without cosponsors, for two years.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Primary committee of referral (chair: Rep. Joe Barton, R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action — no hearing or markup — before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Additional committee of referral (chair: Rep. Bill Thomas, R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received jurisdiction over the bill's tax title and took no action on it during the Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 25, 2005, and never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member signed on, so the partisan split was never tested; the bill had zero cosponsors — including zero Democrats — while both committees that held it were chaired by Republicans who took no action.

industries.note: The bill replaces private health coverage with a public prepaid program for basic care; insurers would lose their core market, though voluntary plans could still act as agents or provide supplementary coverage. Because the bill never advanced, insurers kept the existing system intact.

Providers would gain a universal payer and guaranteed payment, but would accept board-set fee schedules, hospital maximum rates, and payment at the least expensive standard accommodations — trading pricing power for guaranteed volume.

industries.industry: Most commercial businesses (as remitters of the tax)
industries.note: A 5% value-added tax would apply to commercial sales of property and services, raising the cost of goods and services consumers buy; the industry's interest in avoiding the tax runs against the public's interest in funded coverage.

The bill covers prescribed drugs that are unusually expensive as an auxiliary benefit, creating a public payer for high-cost prescriptions; that benefit itself is subject to Board limits when funds are inadequate.
